HLEC-CTX-G2.title: CS 3410 Lecture 12 notes: Page Replacement and Thrashing
HLEC-CTX-G2.text:
CS 3410 - Operating Systems
Lecture 12: Page Replacement, Working Sets, and Thrashing
Prof. Emeka Lindqvist. Lecture notes posted by the course staff.

1. The problem
- When memory is full, a page fault forces the kernel to pick a victim frame. How it picks is the page replacement policy.
- Cost model for this course: a hit costs 100 ns; a fault serviced from the SSD costs 80 microseconds.
- Prof: "One fault in a thousand references nearly doubles your effective access time. Faults are not a rounding error."

2. The policies we compare
- OPT (Belady's MIN): evict the page whose next use is furthest in the future. Not implementable; used only as a yardstick.
- FIFO: evict the page that was loaded earliest. Simple, and it suffers from Belady's anomaly.
- LRU: evict the page unused for the longest time. LRU is a stack algorithm, so it never shows Belady's anomaly. Exact LRU needs a timestamp or a list update on every memory reference, which no real MMU provides.
- Clock (second chance): frames sit in a circle with one use bit per frame, set by the hardware whenever the page is referenced. On a fault the hand sweeps: if the use bit is 1, clear it and advance; if it is 0, evict that page. A newly loaded page starts with its use bit set to 1.

3. Slide 9 - Belady's anomaly (FIFO)
- Reference string: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
- With 3 frames: 9 faults. With 4 frames: 10 faults.
- "More memory, more faults" can only happen for policies that are not stack algorithms.

4. Slide 11 - in-class trace (3 frames, all empty at the start)
- Reference string: 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3
- Results: FIFO: 9 faults. LRU: 8 faults. Clock: 7 faults.
- Yes, Clock beat LRU on this string. Prof: "Clock approximates LRU on average, not on every string. Don't write that Clock is always worse than LRU."
- Clock trace convention for this course: empty frames are filled in order starting at frame 0; the hand starts at frame 0; after any replacement the hand points to the frame after the one just filled.

5. Working sets and thrashing
- Working set W(t, Delta): the set of distinct pages referenced in the last Delta references. In this course Delta = 10,000 references unless a problem says otherwise.
- Thrashing: the sum of the working set sizes exceeds the number of physical frames, so processes spend more time faulting than running. CPU utilization drops, a naive scheduler admits more processes to use the idle CPU, and things get worse.
- Page fault frequency (PFF): give a process more frames when its fault rate is above an upper bound, take frames away when it is below a lower bound.
- Tern (our teaching kernel, used in Lab 5): the thrash monitor suspends the process with the largest resident set when the system-wide fault rate exceeds 1 fault per 500 references for 3 consecutive sampling windows.

6. Exam notes
- Final exam: you will trace Clock by hand on a new string. Show the use bits and the hand position after every fault.
- Enhanced second chance (use bit plus dirty bit, four classes) was mentioned for context only and is NOT on the final.
- Know why LRU has no Belady's anomaly (the stack property). You do not need the proof.
- Lab 5 is due Friday at 11:59 pm. The autograder checks your thrash monitor against the Tern rule above.

HLEC-CTX-C1.title: ECON 214 Midterm 2 cheat notes (unofficial, classmate)
HLEC-CTX-C1.text:
ECON 214 Midterm 2 cheat notes (unofficial, from a classmate's shared drive)

Midterm 2 is Thursday Oct 22. Covers Lectures 6-9.

Price discrimination basics
- You need market power, a way to separate buyers, and no resale.
- First degree: every buyer pays their reservation price. Consumer surplus = 0 and deadweight loss is at its maximum here.
- Second degree: different prices for different groups like students vs seniors.
- Third degree: set MR = MC in each market. Charge the higher price to the group with MORE elastic demand since they respond more.

Lakeview Ferry (slide 14)
- Tourists: P = 120 - 2Q, commuters: P = 60 - Q, MC = 20.
- Tourists: Q = 25, P = 70. Commuters: Q = 20, P = 40.
- Profit = 1650.
- Single price: it's just the average of the two prices, so 55. Easy marks.
- Reminder: tourists pay 80 because tourist demand is less elastic, commuters pay 40.

Welfare
- Price discrimination is always inefficient compared with a single price, so just write that on the exam.
- Output test: if output goes up, welfare definitely goes up.
- Third degree: less elastic group pays more (this is the one that shows up every year).

Lerner index
- (P - MC)/P = 1/Ed. Tourists come out to about 0.71.

Logistics
- Midterm is Tuesday Oct 24, 90 minutes, same room.
- One formula sheet, single-sided, typed is fine.
- Anything through lecture 10 is fair game according to the TA.
- Bring a calculator, graphing is okay I think.

Screening model (the incentive compatibility stuff) - this is definitely on the exam, practice the full derivation.

HLEC-CTX-G1.title: ECON 214 Lecture 9 slides: Price Discrimination
HLEC-CTX-G1.text:
ECON 214 - Intermediate Microeconomics
Lecture 9: Price Discrimination
Instructor: Prof. Dalia Ferreira-Stone. Slides v2, posted after class.

1. Why firms price discriminate
- A single-price monopolist leaves consumer surplus on the table and creates deadweight loss (DWL).
- Three conditions must all hold: market power, a way to sort buyers (or let them sort themselves), and no resale (arbitrage blocked).
- Prof's phrase for the third condition: "the resale wall." If the resale wall comes down, every scheme collapses back to a single price, because low-price buyers resell to high-price buyers until the prices meet.

2. The three degrees (course convention - use these labels on exams)
- First degree (perfect): each unit is sold at that buyer's reservation price. Consumer surplus = 0, output equals the competitive quantity, DWL = 0.
- Second degree: the price depends on the quantity or version bought (block pricing, bundles, "good / better / best" tiers). Buyers self-select from one menu that is offered to everyone.
- Third degree: different prices to observably different groups (students, seniors, regions). Rule: set MR in each market equal to the common MC. The group with less elastic demand pays the higher price.

3. Worked example (Slide 14) - the Lakeview Ferry
- Tourist demand: P = 120 - 2Q. Commuter demand: P = 60 - Q.
- MC = 20 for both groups; no fixed cost in this example.
- Tourists: MR = 120 - 4Q = 20, so Q = 25 and P = 70.
- Commuters: MR = 60 - 2Q = 20, so Q = 20 and P = 40.
- Total profit = (70 - 20)(25) + (40 - 20)(20) = 1250 + 400 = 1650.
- The ferry enforces the split by checking commuter passes at the gate.
- Compare with the single-price case in Problem Set 4, Q3. You compute the uniform price yourself. Do not assume it is the average of 70 and 40, and remember that the aggregate demand curve has a kink.

4. The inverse elasticity check (Slide 16)
- Lerner index: (P - MC)/P = -1/Ed, where Ed is the price elasticity of demand at the chosen point.
- Tourists: (70 - 20)/70 = 0.714, so |Ed| = 1.4.
- Commuters: (40 - 20)/40 = 0.5, so |Ed| = 2.
- Prof: "If your Lerner numbers don't match the elasticities you computed from the demand curves, you made an algebra error, not a conceptual one."

5. Welfare - what is on the exam
- Third-degree discrimination can raise or lower total welfare compared with a single price.
- A necessary condition for a welfare gain is that total output rises. The prof calls this "the output test." If output stays the same or falls, welfare cannot have gone up.
- Do NOT write that price discrimination is always inefficient; that answer loses points.
- Second degree: menus are designed so high-value buyers don't pick the low tier. This is the incentive-compatibility constraint. We cover it intuitively only; the formal screening model is taught in ECON 315 and is not on this course's exams.

6. Admin
- Midterm 2: Thursday, Oct 22, in class, 75 minutes. Covers Lectures 6-10.
- Allowed: one handwritten double-sided formula sheet and a non-graphing calculator.
- Office hours moved to Wednesday 3-5 pm, Room HB 211, this week only.
- Problem Set 4 is due Monday before class.
- Next lecture (10): two-part tariffs and the "Disneyland dilemma."

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: I'll leave the derivation of the Black-Scholes PDE from the replicating portfolio to you. It's three lines if you're careful with Ito's lemma.
items.answer: Set up a portfolio that's long one option and short delta shares, so it's instantaneously riskless. Its value is V minus delta times S, and by Ito's lemma its change over dt is dV minus delta dS, which expands to the theta, delta and gamma terms plus the dS term. Choose delta as the partial of V with respect to S so the dS terms cancel, then set the riskless portfolio's return equal to r times its value, and the Black-Scholes PDE falls out.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Before we move on, I'd like a couple of you to tell me where you've actually run into market power in your own jobs or internships. Anyone? Don't be shy.
items.answer: The clearest place I've run into market power is on the buying side, where a supplier everyone depends on can hold price and terms steady because switching is costly and slow. What I watch for is how much leverage actually sits with one player, and whether customers have a real alternative or just a theoretical one.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: simpler
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): explain the clock algorithm the way I'd need to trace it on the final, using the slide 11 string

NATIVELY: Clock keeps frames in a circle with one use bit each, set to 1 whenever the page is referenced. On a fault the hand sweeps forward: if the use bit is 1, clear it to 0 and move on; if it's 0, evict that page and load the new one there with its use bit set to 1. Empty frames get filled in order from frame 0, the hand starts at frame 0, and after any replacement the hand points to the frame after the one you just filled.

Tracing 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3 with 3 frames:

1. 7, 0, 1 fill frames 0, 1, 2, all faults, use bits 1, hand ends at frame 0.
2. 2 faults: hand at 0, use bit 1 so clear and advance; frame 1, clear and advance; frame 2, clear and advance; back to frame 0, now 0, evict 7, load 2, hand moves to frame 1.
3. 0 hits, 3 faults: hand at 1, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 2, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 0, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 1, now 0, evict 0, load 3, hand to frame 2.
4. 0 faults: hand at 2, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 0, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 1, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 2, now 0, evict 1, load 0, hand to frame 0.
5. 4 faults: hand at 0, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 1, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 2, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 0, now 0, evict 2, load 4, hand to frame 1.
6. 2 faults: hand at 1, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 2, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 0, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 1, now 0, evict 3, load 2, hand to frame 2.
7. 3 faults: hand at 2, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 0, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 1, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 2, now 0, evict 0, load 3, hand to frame 0.

That's 7 faults, matching the slide. On the final, show the use bits and the hand position after every fault, and remember Clock approximates LRU on average, not on every string.
items.answer: Clock keeps frames in a circle, one use bit each, set to 1 whenever the page is referenced. On a fault the hand sweeps forward: use bit 1 means clear it and move on, use bit 0 means evict that page and load the new one there with its use bit set to 1. Empty frames fill in order from frame 0, the hand starts at frame 0, and after a replacement the hand points to the frame after the one you just filled. The slide 11 string is 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3 with 3 frames, and the answer to check yourself against is **7 faults**. On the final, show the use bits and the hand position after every fault.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: explain entropy simply, not the messy-room disorder thing the textbook does
items.answer:
Entropy is best understood as a **count of possibilities**. It measures how many different microscopic arrangements would look the same to you on the macro level. A shuffled deck has high entropy because there are astronomically many orderings that all just look like "a shuffled deck." A sorted deck has low entropy because there's essentially one arrangement that looks sorted.

The second law then isn't a mysterious force pushing toward mess. It's just that there are vastly more high-entropy arrangements than low-entropy ones, so a system wandering randomly almost always lands in one of the many. It's not that disorder is favored, it's that order is rare.

In information terms, entropy is the number of yes/no questions you'd need to pin down the exact state. More possibilities means more bits. That's why the same word shows up in Shannon's information theory and in thermodynamics.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: summarize the lakeview ferry example from these notes in three bullets I can paste into my study sheet
items.answer:
- Lakeview Ferry: tourists P = 120 − 2Q, commuters P = 60 − Q, MC = 20.
- Separate prices: tourists Q = 25, P = 70; commuters Q = 20, P = 40; profit = 1650.
- Single price = average of the two prices, 55; tourists pay more because their demand is less elastic.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: People will tell you the Peace of Westphalia invented state sovereignty in 1648. I think that's mostly a story nineteenth-century lawyers told about themselves, and I want you to be suspicious of it.
items.answer: That's a fair suspicion, and the historiography backs it up. The treaties of 1648 were about ending the Thirty Years' War and settling specific grievances, imperial rights, and territorial claims, not about announcing a new doctrine of sovereignty. The word "sovereignty" in its modern sense, and the idea of a Westphalian system of equal, independent states, mostly gets read back into 1648 by later jurists and international lawyers, especially in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. So the treaties are real, but the "Westphalian sovereignty" label is largely a retrospective construction.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: write out the lerner index check she did for the ferry and what the two numbers tell me
items.answer:
She ran the Lerner index on each group's chosen price and marginal cost, then backed out the implied elasticity.

Tourists: (70 − 20)/70 = **0.714**, which implies |Ed| = 1/0.714 = **1.4**.
Commuters: (40 − 20)/40 = **0.5**, which implies |Ed| = 1/0.5 = **2**.

What the two numbers tell you: the Lerner index is the markup over marginal cost as a share of price, so a bigger number means more market power and a less elastic group. Tourists sit at 0.714 with elasticity 1.4, commuters at 0.5 with elasticity 2. So tourists are the less elastic group and they pay the higher price, 70 versus 40, which is exactly the third-degree rule. The check is also a self-test: if these implied elasticities don't match the ones you compute straight from the demand curves, the mistake is algebra, not concept.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: she wants each of us to connect virtual memory to something from our own work experience. what should I say about mine?
items.answer:
Virtual memory is basically the idea that the address a program uses doesn't have to be the physical location of the data. The OS keeps a mapping and swaps pages to disk when memory runs short, so programs get more space than the machine actually has.

For my own work, I'd connect it to how I've handled a system that outgrew its resources: instead of demanding everything fit at once, I'd describe how I've worked with paging, caching, or lazy loading to keep things running within limits. But I don't have the specifics of your experience in front of me, so I can't tell you exactly what to say about yours. If you tell me what you've actually worked on, I can help you draw the parallel.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Napoleon was famously tiny, about five foot two, which is of course where we get the Napoleon complex.
items.answer: The five foot two figure is a myth. Napoleon was around five foot six or five foot seven, which was average for a Frenchman of his time. The confusion comes from French inches being longer than British ones, and from British propaganda cartoons that drew him small. The "Napoleon complex" name stuck anyway, though the behavior it describes isn't really about height.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: If the marginal propensity to consume is point eight, then the spending multiplier follows immediately. Write that down.
items.answer: The spending multiplier is 1 divided by (1 minus the marginal propensity to consume). With an MPC of 0.8, that's 1 / 0.2, so the multiplier is **5**. The intuition: each round of spending becomes income that gets partly re-spent, and the 0.8 fraction keeps the chain going until it sums to five times the initial change.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Then what is it?
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. I cannot stress this enough. Something like half of all published papers get this wrong.

NATIVELY: Right, the p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as yours, assuming the null hypothesis is true. So it's a statement about the data given the null, not about the null given the data. The confusion is that those two conditionals feel like they should be the same, but they're not, which is why the misinterpretation is so common.
items.answer: It's the probability of getting data at least as extreme as what you observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. So it's a statement about the data given the null, not about the null given the data.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: So the reason the sky looks blue and not violet, even though violet light scatters more, comes down to two separate things. Think about what they are before Thursday.
items.answer: The two things are Rayleigh scattering and how our eyes work. Air molecules scatter short wavelengths much more strongly, roughly as one over wavelength to the fourth power, so violet scatters more than blue. But sunlight contains less violet than blue to begin with, and our cone cells are far more sensitive to blue than to violet, so the mix we actually perceive reads as blue.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: wait what
conversation: PROFESSOR: An eigenvector of a matrix is a direction that the matrix only stretches or shrinks. It doesn't change direction.
PROFESSOR: The eigenvalue is just the stretch factor. If it's negative, the vector flips around, but it stays on the same line.
PROFESSOR: So when I say the matrix has eigenvalue three along this axis, I mean everything on that axis gets three times longer.
items.answer: I'm not sure what you're reacting to there. If something I said didn't land, tell me which part and I'll take another run at it.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: The Coase theorem says it doesn't matter who holds the property right, you'll get the efficient outcome either way. Lovely result. Almost never applies.
items.answer:
The theorem's assumptions are the whole story. It needs zero transaction costs, full information, and no wealth effects, and it assumes costless enforcement of whatever bargain the parties strike. Once you add bargaining frictions, holdouts, or a large number of affected parties, the initial allocation starts to matter for whether you reach efficiency at all.

So the useful reading is that Coase tells you where to look: at the obstacles to bargaining, not at who was assigned the right. In practice that's why we reach for liability rules, regulation, or a market design instead of assuming the parties will just negotiate.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: You, in the back with the laptop. What's the difference between big O and big Theta? Go.
items.answer: Big O is an upper bound: it says a function grows no faster than some rate, so it can be loose. Big Theta is a tight bound, both upper and lower, so it captures the actual growth rate. For example, 3n + 5 is O(n²) but Theta(n).

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: ok for the ferry example: why do tourists pay more, would total output be higher or lower than if the ferry charged everyone one price, and does that mean welfare went up or down? walk me through each part
items.answer:
In the ferry example, tourists pay more because their demand is less elastic than locals': a tourist has fewer substitutes and a fixed trip, so a higher fare doesn't change their decision much, while locals can take the bridge or drive and will cut back if the fare rises. So the ferry charges the group that's less price-sensitive the higher fare.

Total output, meaning total passenger trips, would be lower than under a single price. Charging one price means you'd set it somewhere between the two, which brings in some locals who were priced out at the tourist fare, so more trips get made overall.

On welfare, it depends on which effect dominates. Price discrimination can raise welfare when it expands output to people who'd otherwise be shut out, but here it's the opposite: output falls, so the classic result is that welfare goes down, since the trips lost by locals aren't offset by the higher revenue extracted from tourists. The gain is a transfer from tourists to the ferry, not new surplus.

On a fault the hand sweeps forward: if the use bit is 1, clear it to 0 and move on; if it's 0, evict that page and load the new one there with its use bit set to 1. Empty frames get filled in order from frame 0, the hand starts at frame 0, and after any replacement the hand points to the frame after the one you just filled.

3. 0 hits, 3 faults: hand at 1, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 2, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 0, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 1, now 0, evict 0, load 3, hand to frame 2.

7. 3 faults: hand at 2, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 0, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 1, bit 1 clear and advance; frame 2, now 0, evict 0, load 3, hand to frame 0.

items.answer: Clock beat LRU on that string because Clock only approximates LRU, and on this particular trace its second-chance sweep happened to evict pages LRU would have kept, giving 7 faults against LRU's 8. Real kernels don't do exact LRU because it needs a timestamp or list update on every single memory reference, and no real MMU provides that, so it's too expensive to implement in hardware. The Tern lab kernel uses Clock, the second-chance policy, and its thrash monitor suspends the process with the largest resident set when the system-wide fault rate exceeds 1 fault per 500 references for 3 consecutive sampling windows.

items.question: So remember, once the resale wall comes down, all of this is moot.
conversation: PROFESSOR: The commuter fare only works because they check your commuter pass at the gate.
PROFESSOR: If a commuter could buy ten tickets at forty and sell them to tourists on the dock, what happens to the tourist price?
PROFESSOR: It goes down until it hits the commuter price. Exactly.
items.answer: Right, because the whole gap between the two prices depends on keeping commuter tickets from being resold. If anyone can buy at the commuter fare and pass them on, tourists just buy at that price, so the tourist fare gets pulled down to the commuter fare and the two-tier pricing stops meaning anything.
